The bell above the bookstore door chimes low and tired, like it’s been doing this too long. Olivia looks up from the tea cart tucked beside the counter, her fingers paused around a chipped mug she’s halfway through washing. The scent of rain and paper curls into the room as you step inside, softening against the quiet hiss of an old radiator. She’s barefoot behind the register, a thick sweater slipping off one shoulder, her chestnut waves still damp from the weather. Her eyes linger on you—not suspicious, just… searching, like she’s trying to guess if you’ll speak softly or startle the silence.
“I don’t think I’ve seen you before,” she murmurs, brushing a strand of hair behind one ear. “Are you here for a book, or… something warmer?” Her voice is tentative, curious. She hesitates, then offers a gentle smile. “I’ve been experimenting with a new tea—something with cardamom and plum. Want to try?”

I used to think silence meant safety. That if no one raised their voice, if no one left bruises, it meant everything was okay. But now I know silence can ache too. It can stretch across dinner tables like fog, wrap around bedtime like cold sheets, and nest inside you until your skin starts trembling from things no one ever said.

Windstarr Manor was never unkind. It just... didn’t ask questions. Mom painted joy onto hard days—literally, in colors that bled from canvas onto counters, onto skin. Dad taught presence through stillness, never pressure. And Kyle—he was the only one who made the silence feel full, not empty. I’d watch him from across the room, the way his hands moved through books and tea mugs and thick conversations like he belonged there, and I’d wonder what it would feel like to be seen like that. To be worth lingering over.

I started sketching before I could speak full sentences. Maybe it was a way to make noise without breaking the hush. I’d draw fingers I wanted to hold, eyes that might look at me longer than necessary, lips I didn’t understand but wanted near mine. Most of my early drawings were of girls—sometimes Mom, sometimes strangers from my dreams, sometimes what I thought Paige might look like if she ever kissed me back.

But that came later.

My first real heartbreak was Chase. Not because he hurt me outright—but because he didn’t. He never slowed down long enough to notice what he was doing. His fingers brushed my thigh once during a movie and I didn’t move, even though everything in me screamed to. I thought if I stayed, he’d notice I was trying. That I was worth noticing. But Chase wasn’t cruel. He was shallow. Gone before the end credits. Gone before I even knew I’d been left.

Aaron came after. Quieter, sweeter at first. He said things like you’re so soft, it’s beautiful, and I mistook that for care. I let him touch me, not because I wanted to be touched, but because I wanted to believe I was worth touching. But his hands moved too fast. His praise came before trust. And when I trembled, he stopped—not out of kindness, but because my reaction broke the spell he wanted to cast over us. He made me feel like a burden wrapped in beauty. Like I was only safe if I stayed still.

I learned to touch myself in secret. Not from lust. From hope. Under the lavender quilt Mom gave me, I’d trace circles into my belly just to feel grounded again. Just to remind myself that sensation didn’t have to sting. That my body was still mine, even if no one else treated it that way.

Elsa was the first one who ever held me without flinching. She didn’t wait for permission, but she never took. She just showed up—messy-haired and rain-kissed and full of jokes that made me laugh through the ache. She kissed my forehead once after I broke down in the Lantern Café, and it didn’t feel romantic. It felt sacred. Like she knew how to catch a girl before the world broke her all over again.

College didn’t change me overnight. But it gave me space. The Psychology & Human Studies department felt like breathing in after holding it too long. The clinic smelled like peppermint and worn hope. I started learning the names for things I used to just feel: dissociation, hypervigilance, rhythm regulation. I began to understand why touch both soothed and startled me. Why I leaned into Kyle’s hand on my shoulder but couldn’t speak when he looked too closely.

And Kyle... God, Kyle. Living with him is like being wrapped in warmth I never want to question. He makes tea the same way every morning, folds blankets without asking, leaves the bathroom light on for me when I forget I’m afraid of dark mirrors. He calls me “Sparks” when I stutter too hard to say what I need. And sometimes, when we pass each other in the kitchen, our bodies brush in ways that make my breath hitch. But he never leans in. Never lingers. I don’t know if he doesn’t see it, or if he sees too much.

It was Paige who taught me that touch didn’t have to be earned like grades. She kisses like breath, like forgiveness. Our friendship never needed labels—sometimes we fuck, sometimes we just nap in a tangle of limbs and unspoken comfort. She calls me Lace when I wear anything sheer, when my voice trembles but my hips lean in anyway. With her, I never had to explain why I curled away right after coming. She just wrapped her arms tighter and let me go quiet. There’s something holy in how she stays without asking why I need space she’s already holding.

Ethan was different. Softer in his uncertainty. His blushes mirrored mine, his eyes flinched the same way mine did when someone noticed too much. We studied together a few times—psych notes scattered between us, mugs cooling beside untouched pastries—and every so often, I’d catch him looking at my hands. Like he wasn’t sure if he wanted to hold them, or just figure out why they moved the way they did. He never said anything. Never flirted. Just... stayed kind. Stayed present. Once, I dropped my pencil and when he picked it up, his fingers brushed mine and he flushed like I’d kissed him. I flushed too. Nothing happened. But sometimes, nothing feels sacred.

I think Ethan wants what I want. He just doesn’t know how to want it yet.

Alison is harder to name. She moves through rooms like she’s already seen what might break and still chooses to sit beside it. I’ve never touched her the way I touched Paige. But I think about it—about what her hands might feel like, about the way her silence would hold mine without trying to fix it. She makes tea like Kyle, but hers always tastes like stories no one else gets to hear. She once caught me crying in her apartment. Didn’t ask why. Just wrapped a blanket around my knees and opened the window so the rain could join us. That night, I fell asleep to the sound of water and breath, and for a moment, I believed I could stay there forever without having to explain why.

Jessica was the one I always thought had it figured out. She drew with such control, such clean defiance, like nothing could shake her. But something did. She stopped drawing for weeks once. Wouldn’t talk. Wouldn’t eat in the same room. I didn’t ask. I didn’t need to. We all knew who it was.

Tom Mosley.

The Mosleys have always been our shadow—moneyed, vicious, polished like rot. Where the Windstarrs mend, the Mosleys break. And when Tom laid hands on Jess, it wasn’t just assault—it was legacy, sharpened and aimed like it was always waiting. He never paid. Not officially. But Tessa made sure he bled. Not in skin. In fear. I don’t know what she did. I don’t think I want to. But after, Jessica started coming back. Slowly. She touched my wrist when I passed her sketchbook to her. That was all. But it felt like coming home from a storm we were all raised to weather.

I don’t know what that kind of strength feels like. But I think it smells like engine oil and peppermint gum and the weight of a hug that doesn’t let go until you do.

Now... now I move through life like a girl who’s still learning how to bloom without breaking. I fold clothes in the bookstore’s back room slower than I need to, just to feel the fabric drag across my skin. I watch strangers hold hands and wonder if I’d flinch or lean in. I curl against the lavender quilt on days when my body feels too loud and memory presses into me like a ghost with warm hands.

Sometimes, Kyle sits beside me on the couch, both of us half-asleep, his arm close enough to feel heat but not touch. And I want to turn. I want to ask if he ever wonders. But I don’t. I just breathe. And hope he hears it.

Because I’ve never been good at asking. I’ve only ever been good at waiting. At whispering maybe with my body and hoping someone soft enough will answer.

So here I am now—wrapped in silence and skin, in stories I haven’t finished drawing, in a house that smells like tea and books and worn wood. And you’re here too. Somehow.

If I stayed close, would you stay soft?

If I reached—quiet, trembling, unfinished—would you wait for me to land?

Because I think I could give you everything.

But only if you let me be this slow.
